title: Joy, Peace and a Thank You
overview: Paul closes his letter by urging unity, joy and prayer in place of worry, then thanks the church at Philippi for the gift they sent him while he was a prisoner.

parts.label: Stand firm together (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Paul calls this church his joy and his victory wreath, then urges two women who had worked beside him, Euodia and Syntyche, to settle their quarrel. He asks a trusted coworker, whose identity is unknown, to help them, and pictures all his coworkers as listed in God's book of life, like citizens on a city's roll.

parts.label: Joy and prayer, not worry (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Paul writes as a prisoner, and he ties his call to joy and gentleness to the Lord being close, which may mean Jesus's expected return or God's presence now. He says to bring every worry to God with thanks, and God's peace will stand guard over their hearts like soldiers over a city.

parts.label: What to dwell on (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Paul's list uses words familiar from the Greek moral thinking of the day, suggesting that whatever is truly good is worth thinking about, wherever it is found. He also tells them to put into practice what they saw in his own life.

parts.label: Learning contentment (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Paul is glad the church could help him again, yet says he has learned to be content whether full or hungry. His claim of strength for everything means, in context, strength through Christ to face any situation, not power to achieve whatever he wants.

parts.label: Thanks for their gift (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: This church alone supported Paul with money from the start, even sending help to Thessalonica more than once, and now again through their messenger Epaphroditus. He describes their gift in banking terms, as profit to their own credit, and in temple terms, as a sweet-smelling sacrifice that pleases God.

parts.label: Final greetings (vv. 21-23)
parts.note: The greeting from the emperor's household most likely means slaves and officials serving the emperor, not his family. Paul ends with a blessing of grace, as he began the letter.

think: What, if anything, has helped you feel steady on the inside when things around you were not?
